name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Don’t eat the candy!
description: Voters beware! At the end of your ballot, you’re asked to approve permanent changes to the North Carolina constitution that will harm families for generations. In particular, a proposed amendment to cap local property taxes looks appealing, but it’s really a gift to data centers, Duke Energy and Raleigh politicians. The ballot question reads, “For […]
text:
Wording of the proposed property tax amendment on the North Carolina's  2026 NC general election ballot. (Photo: Laura Leslie/NC Newsline) Voters beware! At the end of your ballot, you’re asked to approve permanent changes to the North Carolina constitution that will harm families for generations.
In particular, a proposed amendment to cap local property taxes looks appealing, but it’s really a gift to data centers, Duke Energy and Raleigh politicians.
The ballot question reads, “For or Against: Constitutional amendment requiring limits on property tax increases by local governments.”
But if it passes, the actual sentence added to the constitution reads, “The General Assembly shall enact general laws limiting the amount by which the levy of taxes on property may increase, which may include exceptions.”
That last phrase – “which may include exceptions” – opens the door for super-sized property owners to lobby state legislators for special tax breaks and extra protection the rest of us won’t get.
In other words, the amendment not only gives control of local property taxes to politicians in Raleigh; it also tells them they can hand out favors to whoever they want.
The big winners will be corporate owners with lobbyists and campaign money to attract the attention of political leaders.
In Wake County, as in many other counties, Duke Energy is the biggest property taxpayer, followed by tech giants, drug makers, banks, and major office park/apartment owners.  Wolfspeed Inc., the data center chipmaker, ranks first in Durham County, followed by Eli Lilly & Company.
Corporate owners lead city and county lists across the state, from Alamance to Wilson.  And they provide a crucial share of the tax revenue needed to finance public services, as they should.
The top 25 property taxpayers in Wake County pay more than 33,000 families in homes worth $400,000.  You can understand why corporations will lobby for special treatment if this amendment passes.
And they’ll find a way to win.  Ten years ago, IBM and its data center in the Research Triangle Park outranked Wolfspeed as the number one property taxpayer in Durham County.  Today, IBM has dropped off the top 25 list, due to its persistent litigation and lobbying.
Even if the legislature doesn’t pick favorites for “exceptions” and instead limits everyone’s tax payment, we will still lose.  The big taxpayers will benefit the most and leave a giant hole in local budgets.  We’ll have to fill the hole with higher fees and sales taxes that hit low- and middle-income families hardest – or we lose the funds needed for public safety, schools, water and sewer service, etc.
Voter Guide: 2026 NC voter guide

Like many civic groups, the nonpartisan League of Women Voters recommends that voters oppose the property tax amendment.  LWV says it “would shift greater authority over local funding decisions to the state while leaving the actual limits, formulas and possible exceptions to future legislation.”
Another constitutional amendment on our ballot would cap the state’s income tax rate at 3.5%.  The cap bans a system that taxes the super-rich and corporations at a higher rate than moderate-income residents – and will force increases in service fees and sales taxes.
Earlier this year, Missouri voters defeated a so-called tax reform referendum after a months-long campaign exposed it would primarily benefit billionaires and “stick each working family with a bill of about $500 more each year.”
We have very little time to spread the truth about the harmful impact of the tax amendments on our ballot.
The NC Budget and Tax Center points out that the property tax amendment doesn’t guarantee a lower tax rate for homeowners; it just gives state legislators authority to pick who gets relief and who pays more.
The center also estimates the income tax amendment could eventually require replacing lost revenue with higher sales taxes that cost the average working family over $900 a year.
Spread the word far and wide.  Go to https://ncvoteagainst.org to learn more.
Like Halloween candy offered by a suspicious stranger, voters have good reason to reject proposals that look good on the surface, but actually give more power to state politicians and wealthy corporations at our expense.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Property tax debate should focus on addressing assessed value
description: Property taxes are a perennial thorn in the side of Indiana lawmakers. The state doesn’t receive any of the revenue, but legislators write the rules that infuriate citizens. Many residents agree on one thing: the assessment system for properties needs to be revamped. Hoosiers deserve some stability in these values that play dramatically into their […]
text:
Hundreds of Hoosiers attended a property tax rally on March 17, 2025, urging lawmakers to provide relief after back-to-back increases. (Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Property taxes are a perennial thorn in the side of Indiana lawmakers. The state doesn’t receive any of the revenue, but legislators write the rules that infuriate citizens.
Many residents agree on one thing: the assessment system for properties needs to be revamped. Hoosiers deserve some stability in these values that play dramatically into their tax bills.
It came up numerous times at a Tuesday night property tax event — in public comments and when I spoke privately with residents. And yet there was no discussion about how to deal with it.
For some, nothing but a complete elimination of property taxes will ever be enough. I am not talking to those people. You simply can’t eliminate $10.6 billion in taxes without replacing it. And replacing the revenue — or even most of it, for those who believe local governments are spending too much — would have disastrous impacts on local services and debt.
That’s because property taxes are stable compared to income and sales taxes. The latter taxes drop when the economy does. During a recession, the police still have to be paid. Schools still have to be open.
Lawmakers to study property tax assessments ahead of 2027 session

But people upset with the mechanics of property taxes and looking for improvements deserve fair consideration. And that’s what brings me to assessed value.
My own home saw its assessed value grow by double-digit percentages year after year. Then in 2022, a fourth such increase caused us to appeal. We had coincidentally performed a private appraisal a few months before for a home equity line of credit. The difference between the county assessment and the appraisal was about $95,000.
So, we appealed and won. But not everyone can afford to pay for an independent appraisal to do that.
In the 2026 legislative session, only three bills involving assessment of property were filed and none of them received a hearing.
House Bill 1238, authored by Rep. Ryan Dvorak, D-South Bend, was the most on point. It would have limited assessed value changes for owner-occupied homesteads to only when a property is sold. The cost of the proposal was huge, though. It would have reduced gross assessed values statewide by $34 billion, causing tax rates to increase and shifting taxes from homesteads to other properties such as rentals, farmers and businesses.
Another bill would have created a special property assessment task force. Instead, legislative leaders simply assigned the general topic to the Interim Study Committee on Fiscal Policy.
An Oct. 14 hearing is set to consider alternatives to the annual adjustment or trending process and the use of cost tables in property assessment. I hope lawmakers consider some smaller changes that would limit the annual growth of assessed value so that the system is more stable, rather than roller coaster swings up and down.
The only reason I can theorize why legislators haven’t tackled the assessed value issue is they don’t want history to repeat itself.
In 1997, the Indiana Tax Court case ruled Indiana’s “true tax value” assessment system unconstitutional. That system relied on subjective cost schedules and formulas that did not measure actual fair market value or property wealth equitably — resulting in unfair assessments across the board that treated taxpayers differently.
As a result, Indiana was forced to adopt a market value system using verifiable data. What this means in practice is using the value of similar properties that have sold to set your assessed value even if you have no intention of selling.
Talk about a rock and a hard place.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: We’re asking the right questions about CT education, but is it enough?
description: The question should not simply be whether Connecticut increases the ECS formula, but whether that reflects the actual cost of educating a child.
text:
​The members of Connecticut’s Blue Ribbon Commission on Education Funding deserve credit for their hard work. It’s an uphill battle.
​For months, the commission has been digging into the mechanics of how education funding actually reaches students. The recent discussion around the Education Cost Sharing (ECS) formula demonstrates a willingness to confront issues that many have avoided for years.
​As a Bridgeport Board of Education member representing the state’s largest and highest-need urban school district, the latest meeting of the commission left me encouraged, yet concerned that we may still be underestimating the magnitude of the challenges facing districts like Bridgeport.
​The commission’s sample scenarios explored increasing the ECS foundation, expanding poverty weights, and adding a special education weight. More importantly, commissioners repeatedly returned to an important question, is it enough?
​The question should not simply be whether Connecticut increases the ECS foundation from one number to another, but whether the foundation reflects the actual cost of educating a child in Connecticut today.
​Let’s run the sample numbers through using my beloved City of Bridgeport and its 20,000 students. New Haven, Hartford, New Britain, New London, Waterbury, Meriden, and others, take note; many of your districts will be similarly impacted.  Run your numbers.
​In the 2027/2028 school year, Bridgeport faces an estimated $25 million loss of one-time revenue alongside approximately $15 million in recurring cost increases. That creates a $40 million structural need before any discussion of new programs or expanded services. $40 million over last year is break-even; we won’t even be able to purchase an additional pencil.
​Under the commission’s model, Bridgeport would receive roughly $23 million in additional recurring ECS funding if all sample reforms were adopted. That helps substantially, but it still leaves a gap of nearly $17 million.
​Districts like Bridgeport are fighting for the survival of public education amid rising special education costs, increased transportation expenses, runaway healthcare inflation, and labor contracts for our underpaid workforce.
​Several commissioners questioned whether the foundation amount adequately reflects current costs, noting that distributing supplemental aid outside the ECS formula may simply codify existing structural funding issues rather than create meaningful new revenue. These are exactly the questions the commission should be asking.
​Implementation is another pressing concern. Assuming the commission recommends a higher foundation amount, increased poverty funding, and additional special education support, this best-case scenario still leaves districts significantly short today. That reality becomes even more troubling if increases are phased in over several years. Bridgeport’s $40 million challenge is not being phased in, nor are rising special education, transportation, or healthcare costs. The bills arrive every day.
​Legislative leaders responsible for balancing the state budget reminded commissioners that education spending competes with other priorities. That is where the commission needs to push back hardest. The commission’s task must be to first determine the overall fiscal needs of CT’s 500,000 students, not adhere to an artificial ceiling under today’s inequitable tax structure.
​If Connecticut determines the current foundation amount is inadequate, equity should not become a long-term goal; it must become an urgency. A district cannot pay this year’s bills with funding promised in 2032.
​Another issue deserves greater attention: how Connecticut measures a community’s ability to pay. The current ECS formula relies heavily on property wealth. Many municipalities today are property rich, but cash-poor. They have substantial grand lists on paper, yet struggle with high poverty, tax-exempt properties, aging infrastructure, and residents with limited income.
​Commissioners discussed whether Connecticut should revisit the 70% property wealth and 30% income wealth weighting that drives ECS allocations. The ratio should be closer to a 50/50 split, if not totally inverted. An equity-based funding system must recognize the actual capacity of residents to support public education through local taxation.
​Accountability is also critical. Taxpayers, families, educators, and policymakers deserve to know that education dollars are being spent wisely. Increased funding and accountability are not mutually exclusive responsibilities, but accountability cannot deflect the state’s responsibility to adequately fund our schools.
​The tale of two Connecticut education systems cannot continue to be our story. We cannot celebrate the success of some while ignoring that high-need districts spend thousands less per pupil than wealthy communities, nor allow cost concerns to distract from the state’s moral and constitutional obligation to provide all children with an adequate education.
​Ultimately, adequacy and equity must remain the guiding principles. Let the legislature figure out how to pay for it, either by dropping guardrails, reducing spending elsewhere, fixing the tax structure or any combination.
​The Blue Ribbon Commission demonstrates a growing consensus that small adjustments over time are not enough. Free from the constraints of a poorly designed survey they did not create, and an expert they did not choose, the commission is asking the right questions and must come up with firm numbers that close the gap for all districts.  Now the governor and legislature must accept the answers, even if they require us to invest more deeply in the students who need it most.
​For Bridgeport and districts like it, the issue is not whether we can afford educational equity. The question is whether we can afford to continue as a society without it.
Joseph Sokolovic lives in Bridgeport.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Activists demand CT officials enforce the Trust Act
description: Dozens gathered in Meriden on Thursday with a list of demands for CT officials, including strengthening the Trust Act and its enforcement.
text:
More than 100 people gathered across the street from the Meriden courthouse Thursday evening with a list of demands for state officials, including strengthening the Trust Act and its enforcement and $50 million in legal support for those affected by immigration enforcement.
The rally came as a response to an arrest at the courthouse on Sept. 23, which raised questions about the legality of ICE’s actions under the state’s Trust Act and other laws. The federal agents were masked and at the courthouse with an administrative, not judicial, warrant — potentially in violation of the law. 
Activists and local politicians who spoke at the rally urged the state to enforce and strengthen the Trust Act, create uniform protocol for how state and local officers should interact with ICE, and investigate any possible collusion between ICE and state court marshals and police. Some also questioned the legality of actions taken by court marshals during last week’s arrest.
The rally was organized by a coalition of activists and attended by groups from across the state, including Middlesex Immigrant Rights Alliance, Danbury Unites for Immigrants, Middlesex Indivisible, Hartford Deportation Defense and CT 50501.

Organizer Miguel Castro, with MIRA, speaks during a Rally Against ICE outside the Meriden Courthouse on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

“All of us are familiar with the Trust Act and the highlights of what it stands for,” Miguel Castro, an organizer of the event and the second vice chair of the Connecticut Hispanic Democratic Caucus and member of MIRA, said. “They write the law, and now one thing is to implement it.”
Attendees chanted “shame” as speakers recalled the events of last week’s courthouse arrest, including the pepper-spraying of an activist and the masks worn into the courthouse by ICE agents. Many held up signs. Some read “melt ICE” and “due process for all.”

Attendees scream “ICE Out” during a Rally Against ICE outside the Meriden Courthouse on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Meriden council member Yvette Cortez spoke at the rally, urging attendees to fight with love for their community. She said that after the ICE activity last week, the state responded with a shared upset felt by some in the community.
“I’m really grateful that the governor and his office immediately took up phone calls, shared in our outrage, and also agreed to do an investigation,” Cortez said. “Some of the videos indicate that the marshals acted in violation of the Trust Act. I don’t want to make any assumptions, not having been there, not having seen everything, but I do have an expectation that a thorough investigation is completed. I hope that the results of that investigation will be shared with the residents of Meriden, and I hope that anybody who violated it will be held accountable to the fullest extent.”
Cortez said the state police were looking into possible violations of the law, including actions taken by court marshals that may have allowed ICE agents to conduct the arrest in the courthouse without the proper documentation. 
The ACLU of Connecticut told the Connecticut Mirror in a statement that, after administrative review by the organization, there is still an “open question” if last week’s courthouse arrest violated state law.

An attendee holds a hand painted umbrella during a Rally Against ICE outside the Meriden Courthouse on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Because the man arrested by ICE was never in state custody, the organization is unsure if the conduct of court marshals falls under the Trust Act — many of the provisions under the law only apply to people in state custody. The ACLU of Connecticut did obtain a copy of the administrative warrant — not judicial — used in last week’s arrest. 
If the man had been in state custody — like a Connecticut prison — the Trust Act would not allow them to turn the man over to ICE with just an administrative warrant for his arrest.
“The administrative warrant ACLU-CT obtained in connection with last Wednesday’s Meriden courthouse arrest raises more questions than it answers,” a statement from David McGuire, Executive Director for the ACLU-CT, read. “Rather than providing clarity, it leaves Connecticut’s immigrant community more vulnerable and uncertain of how protected they are in Connecticut.”
In the statement, McGuire also stressed the need to enforce state law. 
“Last week’s events show that protections on paper only matter if they hold up in practice and are truly enforceable,” McGuire said in the statement. “Together, the Meriden courthouse attack and these incoming protections create an urgent need for state agencies and legislators to review our existing protections and enforcement options, and ACLU-CT will continue working with partners and legislators to make sure all Connecticut residents are truly protected and feel safe where they live.”
Castro and Cortez said the state was complying with their requests to initiate an investigation. During the rally, speakers thanked Gov. Ned Lamont and Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz for “standing up against ICE.”
“We haven’t had any pushback from our state officials, including the governor and the lieutenant governor, who have been instrumental and critical, especially when initiating the investigation and supporting our efforts to protect members of our community,” Castro said.
A request for comment from ICE after the Meriden arrest went unanswered.
The rally follows a press conference Thursday morning, when advocates and elected officials discussed new protections and cuts to services going into effect Oct. 1 that affect the state’s immigrant community.
The new state law that designates “protected areas” like hospitals, schools and places of worship went into effect Thursday, and refugees, asylum seekers and victims of human trafficking now are no longer eligible for Medicaid in Connecticut.
Sen. Matthew Lesser, D-Middletown, co-chair of the Human Services Committee, said that state lawmakers stepped up last legislative session.
“We are laser-focused on keeping our communities safe, and there is nothing that helps make our communities safe when you have federal agents poking around our schools, our churches and mosques and synagogues, our healthcare facilities and our courthouses,” he said.

Brothers Patrick Leonard, left, 15, and Andrew Leonard, 17, of Berlin, hold signs while attending a Rally Against ICE outside the Meriden Courthouse with their mother Michelle Leonard on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

But Lesser also also addressed the enforcement of the Trust Act and of the new laws.
“I think we are going to ask the tough questions of our judicial branch to see what they can and can’t do, and if we need to tweak the law going forward, we can do so,” Lesser said.
Rep. Hubert Delaney, D-Stamford, said that government officials and advocates “have a responsibility to make clear that due process, dignity and the rule of law are still the standard here in Connecticut.”
But even as the new law goes into effect, some immigrant families are being impacted by the loss of health coverage. Lesser said this will affect some 3,200 Connecticut residents, including:
“600 folks who are lawful refugees in this country, 400 folks who have asylum. We have 500 victims of Vladimir Putin’s aggression in Ukraine who are losing their health care today, and it should be no surprise that the man who used the resources of the federal government to try to protect Jeffrey Epstein and his friends has decided to take health care away from survivors of human trafficking. There are dozens of people in Connecticut who are survivors, documented survivors of human trafficking, who are going to lose their healthcare benefits in Connecticut today because of the actions of this administration.”
On Thursday morning, Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., called it “fiscally stupid,” because it will keep people from getting preventative care.
“What an abomination, that we are cutting off healthcare for people that are legal residents of our community,” he said at a press conference in the Legislative Office Building in Hartford. “It betrays the very nature of what it means to be American.”

title: The promise of a free education is fundamental to our democracy
description: The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia announced a lawsuit last week over the unconstitutional underfunding of public schools. I’m not exaggerating when I say this may be the most important case we have filed in my 10 years with this organization. The promise of a free education is fundamental to our democracy itself. […]
text:
During the 2022-23 school year, West Virginia’s average per-pupil expenditure was $14,909 — a total that includes state, local and federal money. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia announced a lawsuit last week over the unconstitutional underfunding of public schools. I’m not exaggerating when I say this may be the most important case we have filed in my 10 years with this organization.
The promise of a free education is fundamental to our democracy itself. It’s so vital that it was enshrined as a right in our 1863 state Constitution, and courts have interpreted that right to mean that schools must not only be adequately funded, but also fairly funded from county to county.
And yet, West Virginia sits at or near the bottom of most national rankings. Politicians have blamed schools, teachers and parents for poor educational outcomes, when the true cause is in black and white on the balance sheets.
During the 2022-23 school year, West Virginia’s average per-pupil expenditure was $14,909 — a total that includes state, local and federal money.  While $14,909 was the reported average, the actual amount per student spent by counties ranged from a low of $12,158 in Barbour County to a high of $22,500 in Doddridge.
That gap gets even wider when you look at only the funding within the state’s control. Combined state and local education funding per pupil ranged from $10,542 in Barbour County to $24,924 in Tyler. In a system that requires that education funding be allocated fairly, some counties receive double the funding of others — not only presenting constitutional concerns, but driving averages up in a way that hides how significantly underfunded many West Virginia counties are.
Across the country, states spend more on education in counties with high rates of students with disabilities and students experiencing poverty because providing quality education to those students is often more expensive. In West Virginia, we do just the opposite: we spend less in counties with the greatest need, and more in counties with higher property wealth. 
Chief among the many flaws in West Virginia’s school funding system is the failure to account for special education services. West Virginia’s special education funding is worse than it was decades ago. Because these services are required by law, failure to provide sufficient funding means that school districts need to dip into funding that would otherwise be used for general education services, or to cover the costs of keeping schools operational.
Looking beyond the funding formula, and including all state grants and special education funding, West Virginia provided an average of $8,057 per student. When the state doesn’t pay enough, counties are left to foot the bill. And a county like Lincoln will never be able to generate enough local wealth to operate the school system that students deserve. Counties generate local revenue for schools primarily through the general school levy, with statewide rates established by the Legislature, and optional excess levies meant to supplement basic school spending. Because these funding sources are tied to property tax, the amount of revenue available to counties — and the amount that gets spent on students — varies not based on need, but on whether students are being educated in counties with high property wealth.
The last time the courts took up this issue the case became so influential it still bears the name of the judge who decided it: the Recht Decision set the standard for school funding in West Virginia and changed the nationwide conversation about it. Despite these clear legal requirements set by our courts, the current funding system leads to outcomes that are worse than what was declared unconstitutional almost 50 years ago.
The current staffing formula provides Lincoln County with fewer staff than the formula at the time the system was declared unconstitutional. The gap between what counties receive, and what they spend, has widened instead of narrowed. School closures are increasing rapidly, as schools struggle to stay afloat with the meager funding provided by the state.
The law believes — as do I — that every West Virginia child is capable of great things that make our communities stronger, healthier and happier. A thorough and efficient system of free schools is what permits those futures to come to fruition.
After years of neglect by the Legislature, it has become clear that children’s constitutional right to education will be left to erode if the courts don’t demand action and declare that the current system isn’t just immoral — it’s also unconstitutional.

text:
North Carolina public school educators, families, and allies demanded a budget that provides pay raises to teachers and funding to schools at a May 1, 2026 rally. (Photo: Brandon Kingdollar/NC Newsline)School finance officers told a state commission Monday that North Carolina’s complicated funding rules and delayed state budget decisions make it harder for districts to plan and spend money where they need it most. 
The comments came during a panel before the Blue Ribbon Commission on Public Education. The panel included superintendents and finance officers from Alamance-Burlington School System and Mooresville Graded School District, along with administrators from Lincoln Charter School. 
“Public school finance today has never been harder and more complex, ” said Tony Messer, chief finance officer for Alamance-Burlington. 
Messer said after Alamance-Burlington used all of its allotted classroom-teacher positions, the district had about $600,000 remaining in the allotment, but funding rules wouldn’t allow it to be used for other needs. He said the money could have helped cover costs such as exceptional children’s services. 
“If we could get a little more flexibility and maybe loosen up some of the restrictions around that, that will be beneficial for all parties involved,” Messer said. 
Angie Davis, chief financial officer for Mooresville Graded School District, said some reporting requirements ask districts for information state agencies already receive in another form. 
For example, she said, districts must report supplemental-pay data through an annual survey, even though the Department of Public Instruction already receives district accounting data each month. Davis said the State Treasurer’s Office also asks districts to report employee income for health-plan purposes, while the retirement system already receives employee salary information each month. 
“Just from a business standpoint, it’s very inefficient when you’re already supplying that information to different agencies,” Davis said. 
Jonathan Bryant, chief administrator of Lincoln Charter School, said having a state budget in place this year brought certainty after the strain of operating without one the previous fiscal year. 
Robert Taylor, the Wake County superintendent who moderated the panel, said the uncertainty becomes a problem when districts have to approve their own budgets before lawmakers finish theirs. A district could approve its budget and move forward, he said, only to learn months later that the General Assembly had added raises or other spending increases that the district would have to match. 
“The thing that scared us the most is the idea that the General Assembly could come back and decide that they were going to put raises in, but we’ve already punched the ticket on our budget and moved forward,” Taylor said. 
Bipartisan education panel unites NC Gov Stein, Republican leaders amid budget rift

Taylor said districts can absorb some delay, but not indefinitely. State lawmakers are supposed to complete the budget by June 30, he said, and districts can manage a delay into August. By December, he said, the uncertainty becomes much harder to manage. 
“If there’s one thing that I think this commission could lift up, it’s the fact that a late budget has a significant impact on how a school district makes decisions,” Taylor said. 
Rep. David Willis, R-Union, challenged the panel’s characterization of state budget delays, calling it “misinformation.”
“First of all, we always have a state budget, so let’s just clarify that,” Willis said. “Now, it may be last year’s budget, and you may not like that number, but you know what the number is.”
Willis said lawmakers regularly seek input from educators and school officials when writing the budget. He also agreed that the state’s education funding model needs to change.
“I think our model is broken,” Willis said. “Let’s go back to the drawing board and figure out what the funding model should look like.”
